kangaroo-at-2016-student-01.title: Add all three sums
kangaroo-at-2016-student-01.body:
Adding the three sums counts every age twice: $2(T + J + A) = 23 + 24 + 25 = 72$, so $T + J + A = 36$. Then $A = 36 - 23 = 13$, $T = 36 - 24 = 12$, $J = 36 - 25 = 11$. The oldest is Alex with 13.

**Answer: (D) 13**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-01.title: Compare the sums
kangaroo-at-2016-student-01.body:
$J + A = 24$ is one more than $T + J = 23$, so Alex is 1 year older than Tom. $A + T = 25$ is one more than $J + A$, so Tom is 1 year older than Johann. So the ages are $J, J+1, J+2$ with $J + (J + 1) = 23$, $J = 11$; the oldest is $13$.

**Answer: (D) 13**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-03.title: Look at the corners
kangaroo-at-2016-student-03.body:
The condition says that every point of one shore has the same distance $d$ to the other shore — the shores are "parallel curves" (one shore is the set of points at distance $d$ from the other). Straight parallel lines (A) and the smoothly curved bands (C), (D), (E), drawn with constant width, have this property.

In (B) both shores are the same zigzag line, just shifted sideways. At a corner of a zigzag the distance to the other zigzag changes: from the tip of an outer corner, the nearest point of the other shore is much farther away than from a point in the middle of a straight piece (and from an inner corner it is closer). So (B) cannot be such a river.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-03.title: Shifted copies
kangaroo-at-2016-student-03.body:
If you shift a straight line sideways, the distance between the two copies is constant. If you shift a zigzag sideways by $s$, the distance between parallel straight pieces is only $s\sin\alpha$ (where $\alpha$ is the angle of the piece), and at the corners the gap is larger: the width is not constant. The other pictures are not simple sideways shifts but true offset curves of constant width.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-04.title: Difference of squares
kangaroo-at-2016-student-04.body:
$2015 \times 2017 = (2016 - 1)(2016 + 1) = 2016^2 - 1$. The two numbers are consecutive integers, so there is no whole number strictly between them.

**Answer: (A) 0**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-04.title: Small case
kangaroo-at-2016-student-04.body:
Try the same pattern with small numbers: $3 \times 5 = 15$ and $4 \times 4 = 16$; $9 \times 11 = 99$ and $10 \times 10 = 100$. Always $(n-1)(n+1) = n^2 - 1$, one less than $n^2$, so nothing lies in between.

**Answer: (A) 0**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-05.title: Reflect in the line y = x
kangaroo-at-2016-student-05.body:
Swapping $(x, y) \to (y, x)$ is the reflection in the line $y = x$. The kangaroo's head is at the upper right, pointing right (large $x$, large $y$); its tail curls at the left (small $x$); the feet are at the bottom (small $y$).

After the reflection, whatever was far to the right is now high up, and whatever was low is now far to the left: the nose (far right, high) stays at the upper right but becomes the highest point, the feet (lowest points) become the leftmost points, and the tail (far left, fairly low) ends up near the bottom. A reflection also turns the picture over (it is not a rotation). Picture (A) shows exactly this.

**Answer: (A)**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-05.title: Track two points
kangaroo-at-2016-student-05.body:
The tip of the nose has the largest $x$ in the original, so after swapping it has the largest $y$: it must be the highest point of the new picture. The bottom of the feet has the smallest $y$, so after swapping it has the smallest $x$: it must be the leftmost point. Only picture (A) has the nose at the top and the feet at the far left.

**Answer: (A)**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-06.title: Tetrahedron
kangaroo-at-2016-student-06.body:
Four planes in general position bound a tetrahedron, a finite region. Three planes are not enough: three planes through a common point cut space into 8 unbounded "octants" (or, if they are not in general position, into slabs and prisms that are also unbounded) — any region bounded by only three planes is infinite.

**Answer: (B) 4**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-06.title: Compare with the plane
kangaroo-at-2016-student-06.body:
In the plane, 2 lines cannot enclose a region but 3 lines can (a triangle). In space, one more is needed: 3 planes give at most an infinite "corner", and a fourth plane cutting off that corner gives a tetrahedron.

**Answer: (B) 4**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-07.title: Neighbouring triangles
kangaroo-at-2016-student-07.body:
Call the corner circles $a, c, i, g$, the edge-midpoint circles $b, f, h, d$ (going around) and the centre $e$. Every small triangle consists of the centre, one corner and one adjacent edge-midpoint. Going around, consecutive triangles share the centre and one other circle:
$$a + b + e = b + c + e = c + f + e = f + i + e = \dots$$
Comparing neighbours: $a = c$, $b = f$, $c = i$, $f = h$, $i = g$, $h = d$. So all four corners are equal and all four edge midpoints are equal: at most 3 different numbers (corners, edge midpoints, centre).

Three different numbers are possible, e.g. corners 1, midpoints 2, centre 3: every triangle has sum 6.

**Answer: (C) 3**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-07.title: Opposite argument
kangaroo-at-2016-student-07.body:
Each corner circle lies in exactly two triangles, together with its two neighbouring midpoints; each midpoint lies in two triangles with its two neighbouring corners. Moving from one triangle to the next around the centre replaces one circle by another, and since the sums are equal, these two circles carry the same number. So the outer ring alternates between just two values, plus the centre: at most 3, and 3 is achievable.

**Answer: (C) 3**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-08.title: Areas
kangaroo-at-2016-student-08.body:
$S_1$ has width $x$ and height $5 - y$; $S_2$ has width $8 - x$ and height $y$. So $x(5 - y) = (8 - x)y$, i.e. $5x - xy = 8y - xy$, so $5x = 8y$ and $x : y = 8 : 5$.

**Answer: (E) 8:5**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-08.title: Add the white rectangle
kangaroo-at-2016-student-08.body:
Add the white rectangle $x \times y$ in the corner to both: $S_1 + \text{white}$ is $x \times 5$, and $S_2 + \text{white}$ is $8 \times y$. Equal areas give $5x = 8y$, so $x : y = 8 : 5$.

**Answer: (E) 8:5**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-09.title: Divide by x
kangaroo-at-2016-student-09.body:
$x = 0$ is not a solution, so divide by $x$: $x - 4 + \frac{2}{x} = 0$, i.e. $x + \frac{2}{x} = 4$.

**Answer: (E) 4**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-09.title: Vieta
kangaroo-at-2016-student-09.body:
The roots are $x_{1,2} = 2 \pm \sqrt2$ with product $2$. So $\frac{2}{x_1} = x_2$ and $x_1 + \frac{2}{x_1} = x_1 + x_2 = 4$ (the same for $x_2$).

**Answer: (E) 4**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-10.title: Arc lengths to angles
kangaroo-at-2016-student-10.body:
$AB$ passes through $O$, so it is a diameter and the arcs $AP$ and $PB$ together form a half circle of length $36$. The full circle has length $72$, so the arc $BP$ of length 16 corresponds to the central angle $\angle BOP = \frac{16}{72}\cdot 360^\circ = 80^\circ$.

$OP \perp PX$ (radius and tangent), so in the right triangle $OPX$: $\angle OXP = 90^\circ - 80^\circ = 10^\circ$. Since $A, O, B, X$ are collinear, $\angle AXP = \angle OXP = 10^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) $10^\circ$**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-10.title: Secant–tangent angle
kangaroo-at-2016-student-10.body:
The angle between a tangent and a secant from an outside point is half the difference of the intercepted arcs: $\angle AXP = \frac{\text{arc } AP - \text{arc } BP}{2}$ measured in degrees. Arc $AP$ corresponds to $\frac{20}{72}\cdot 360^\circ = 100^\circ$, arc $BP$ to $80^\circ$, so $\angle AXP = \frac{100^\circ - 80^\circ}{2} = 10^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) $10^\circ$**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-11.title: Common value
kangaroo-at-2016-student-11.body:
Call the common value $k$. Then $a = k - 2$, $b = k + 2$, $c = \frac k2$, $d = 2k$. Since $a \ge 1$, $k \ge 3$. Then $d = 2k = k + k > k + 2 = b$, and $b$ is larger than $a$ and $c$. So $d$ is the biggest.

**Answer: (D) $d$**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-11.title: Example
kangaroo-at-2016-student-11.body:
The smallest possibility is $k = 4$ ($c$ must be whole, $a \ge 1$): $a = 2$, $b = 6$, $c = 2$, $d = 8$. For larger $k$ the gap between $d = 2k$ and $b = k + 2$ only grows.

**Answer: (D) $d$**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-12.title: Top = a·b²·c
kangaroo-at-2016-student-12.body:
With bottom row $a, b, c$ the middle row is $ab, bc$ and the top is $ab \cdot bc = a b^2 c$. With $a, b, c \ge 2$ the top must be divisible by a square $b^2 \ge 4$.
- $56 = 2 \cdot 2^2 \cdot 7$, $84 = 3 \cdot 2^2 \cdot 7$, $90 = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5$, $220 = 5 \cdot 2^2 \cdot 11$ all work.
- $105 = 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$ has no square factor greater than 1, so it is impossible.

**Answer: (D) 105**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-12.title: Prime factor count
kangaroo-at-2016-student-12.body:
The top $ab^2c$ has at least 4 prime factors (counted with multiplicity), and some prime appears at least twice. $105 = 3\cdot5\cdot7$ has only 3 prime factors, all different, so it cannot be at the top.

**Answer: (D) 105**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-14.title: 30-60-90 triangle
kangaroo-at-2016-student-14.body:
In the right triangle $ABC$, $\sin\angle BAC = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac12$, so $\angle BAC = 30^\circ$. Since $AB \parallel DC$, $\angle ACD = \angle BAC = 30^\circ$ (alternate angles). Triangle $AXC$ is isosceles with $AX = XC$, so $\angle CAX = \angle ACX = 30^\circ$ — not among (A)–(D).

**Answer: (E) another angle** (it is $30^\circ$)

kangaroo-at-2016-student-14.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2016-student-14.body:
Take $BC = 1$, $AC = 2$, so $AB = \sqrt3$: $A = (0,0)$, $B = (\sqrt3, 0)$, $C = (\sqrt3, 1)$, $D = (0, 1)$. $X = (t, 1)$ with $t^2 + 1 = (\sqrt3 - t)^2$ gives $t = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$. Then $\angle XAB = \arctan\sqrt3 = 60^\circ$ and $\angle CAB = 30^\circ$, so $\angle CAX = 30^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) another angle**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-15.title: Size of the squares
kangaroo-at-2016-student-15.body:
Each square has area $2016 / 56 = 36$, so side 6. The squares form an $m \times n$ grid with $mn = 56$, $m \le n$: $(1, 56), (2, 28), (4, 14), (7, 8)$. Each gives a rectangle $6m \times 6n$: $6 \times 336$, $12 \times 168$, $24 \times 84$, $42 \times 48$. That's 4 rectangles.

**Answer: (B) 4**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-15.title: Count factor pairs
kangaroo-at-2016-student-15.body:
$56 = 2^3 \cdot 7$ has $4 \cdot 2 = 8$ divisors, i.e. 4 unordered factor pairs, so 4 different grid shapes of $6\times 6$ squares.

**Answer: (B) 4**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-16.title: Small triangle on the left
kangaroo-at-2016-student-16.body:
The square has side 1. In the picture the square shares the bottom right vertex of the triangle and its top left vertex lies on the left side of the triangle. To the left of the square, the left side of the triangle, the base and the square's left side form a small right triangle with height 1 and a $60^\circ$ angle at the base, so its base is $\frac{1}{\tan 60^\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$.

The triangle's side is $1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$, and its perimeter is $3 + \frac{3}{\sqrt3} = 3 + \sqrt3$.

**Answer: (B) $3 + \sqrt3$**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-16.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2016-student-16.body:
Put the triangle's left vertex at $(0,0)$; its left side is the line $y = \sqrt3 x$. With side $s$, the square occupies $s - 1 \le x \le s$, $0 \le y \le 1$, and its top left corner $(s - 1, 1)$ lies on $y = \sqrt3 x$: $1 = \sqrt3(s - 1)$, $s = 1 + \frac{\sqrt3}{3}$. Perimeter $3s = 3 + \sqrt3$.

**Answer: (B) $3 + \sqrt3$**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-17.title: Blocks of liars
kangaroo-at-2016-student-17.body:
A knight tells the truth, so both neighbours of a knight are liars. A liar lies, so at least one neighbour of a liar is a knight. Hence:
- no two knights sit next to each other, and
- there are never three liars in a row (the middle one would sit between two liars and would be telling the truth).

So the knights split the circle into blocks of 1 or 2 liars. With $k$ knights there are $k$ blocks, so the number of liars $7 - k$ is between $k$ and $2k$: $k \le 7 - k \le 2k$, i.e. $\frac73 \le k \le 3.5$, so $k = 3$ and there are $4$ liars. (Example: K L K L K L L.)

**Answer: (B) 4**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-17.title: Test the options
kangaroo-at-2016-student-17.body:
- 3 liars, 4 knights: two knights would have to sit next to each other — impossible.
- 5 or 6 liars: with at most 2 knights there would be a block of at least 3 liars — impossible (for 5 liars and 2 knights, the blocks sum to 5 so one has $\ge 3$).
- 4 liars: K L K L K L L works: each knight sits between two liars; each liar has a knight neighbour.

**Answer: (B) 4**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-18.title: Divisibility by 9
kangaroo-at-2016-student-18.body:
A number is congruent to its digit sum modulo 9. So the sum of the three numbers is congruent to $1 + 2 + \dots + 9 = 45 \equiv 0 \pmod 9$: the sum must be divisible by 9. $1500$ has digit sum 6, so it is not divisible by 9; the other four ($1503, 1512, 1521, 1575$) are.

**Answer: (A) 1500**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-18.title: The other sums occur
kangaroo-at-2016-student-18.body:
The other four sums really can be obtained:
$142 + 375 + 986 = 1503$, $152 + 374 + 986 = 1512$, $162 + 374 + 985 = 1521$, $123 + 465 + 987 = 1575$.
But every sum is a multiple of 9 (the digit sum of all nine digits is 45), and 1500 is not.

**Answer: (A) 1500**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-19.title: Fill in step by step
kangaroo-at-2016-student-19.body:
Let the inner point be $m$. The bottom left white triangle has corners $2$, $0$ and the bottom point $p$ next to the corner: $2 + 0 + p \equiv 0$, so $p = 1$.
- The black triangle with corners $0$, $m$, $p = 1$: $m + 1 \not\equiv 0$, so $m \ne 2$.
- The white triangle with corners $0$, $m$ and the left point $q$ of the second row: $q \equiv -m$. The white triangle with corners $m$, $2$ and the right point $r$ of the second row: $r \equiv 1 - m$.
- The top black triangle has corners $q, r, m$: $-m + (1 - m) + m = 1 - m \not\equiv 0$, so $m \ne 1$.

So $m = 0$, and indeed everything can be completed: second row $0, 1$; top $2$; bottom row $2, 1, 2, 2$ (check: all white sums $\equiv 0$, black sums $1, 1, 1$).

**Answer: (A) only 0**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-19.title: Check the three values
kangaroo-at-2016-student-19.body:
Try $m = 2$: the black triangle $0, m, 1$ (the 1 is forced by the white corner triangle) sums to 3 — not allowed. Try $m = 1$: the white triangles force the second row to be $2$ and $0$, and the top black triangle then sums to $2 + 0 + 1 = 3$ — not allowed. $m = 0$ works with the completion above.

**Answer: (A) only 0**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-20.title: Tangent–chord angle
kangaroo-at-2016-student-20.body:
The five angles fill the straight angle at $A$ on one side of the tangent: $5x = 180^\circ$, $x = 36^\circ$.

By the tangent–chord theorem, the angle between the tangent and the chord $AD$ equals the inscribed angle over $AD$ on the other side. The angle between $AD$ and the tangent ray on the side of $E$ is $2x = 72^\circ$, and $B$ lies on the arc on the other side, so $\angle ABD = 72^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) $72^\circ$**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-20.title: Via the arcs
kangaroo-at-2016-student-20.body:
Each angle $x = 36^\circ$ between consecutive chords at $A$ (and between the tangent and $AB$, $AE$) is half of an arc: the arcs $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$, $EA$ are each $72^\circ$, so the five points form a regular pentagon. In a regular pentagon $\angle ABD$ is an inscribed angle over the arc $AD$ not containing $B$, which is arc $DE + EA = 144^\circ$, so $\angle ABD = 72^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) $72^\circ$**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-21.title: When is a power equal to 1?
kangaroo-at-2016-student-21.body:
The base $x^2 - 4x + 5 = (x - 2)^2 + 1$ is always at least 1 (in particular positive). A power $a^b$ with $a > 0$ equals 1 exactly when $a = 1$ or $b = 0$.
- $a = 1$: $(x-2)^2 = 0$, $x = 2$.
- $b = 0$: $x^2 + x - 30 = (x + 6)(x - 5) = 0$, $x = 5$ or $x = -6$.

Three different solutions.

**Answer: (C) 3**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-21.title: Take logarithms
kangaroo-at-2016-student-21.body:
Since the base is positive: $(x^2 + x - 30)\ln(x^2 - 4x + 5) = 0$. So $x^2 + x - 30 = 0$ ($x = 5, -6$) or $x^2 - 4x + 5 = 1$ ($x = 2$). (Base $-1$ with even exponent is impossible because the base is $\ge 1$.)

**Answer: (C) 3**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-22.title: Area = r · s
kangaroo-at-2016-student-22.body:
Join the centre of the circle to the four vertices. This splits the quadrilateral into four triangles, each with a side of the quadrilateral as base and the radius $r$ as height. So the area is $\frac12 r \cdot P$, where $P$ is the perimeter. The circle has area $\frac12 r \cdot (2\pi r)$. Hence
$$\frac{\text{area of quadrilateral}}{\text{area of circle}} = \frac{\frac12 r P}{\frac12 r \cdot 2\pi r} = \frac{P}{2\pi r} = \frac43.$$

**Answer: (E) 4:3**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-22.title: Check with a square
kangaroo-at-2016-student-22.body:
The argument shows that for every quadrilateral with an inner circle, (area ratio) = (perimeter ratio). Check with a square of side 2 around a circle of radius 1: perimeters $8 : 2\pi = 4 : \pi$ and areas $4 : \pi$ — equal, as claimed. So here the area ratio is also $4 : 3$.

**Answer: (E) 4:3**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-23.title: Choose one point per column
kangaroo-at-2016-student-23.body:
The marked points form a $3 \times 3$ grid: $x \in \{1, 2, 3\}$, $y \in \{1, 2, 3\}$. A function's graph contains at most one point in each column, so it passes through at most 3 marked points, and then exactly one in each column. Any three points with different $x$ determine exactly one function $y = ax^2 + bx + c$; it is a genuine quadratic ($a \ne 0$) unless the three points are collinear.

Triples with one point per column: $3^3 = 27$. Collinear ones: the 3 horizontal lines and the 2 diagonals — 5. So $27 - 5 = 22$.

**Answer: (D) 22**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-23.title: Second differences
kangaroo-at-2016-student-23.body:
For values $y_1, y_2, y_3$ at $x = 1, 2, 3$ the leading coefficient is $a = \frac{y_1 - 2y_2 + y_3}{2}$. We need $y_1 + y_3 \ne 2y_2$. For $y_2 = 1$: $y_1 + y_3 = 2$ only for $(1,1)$ — 8 good pairs; $y_2 = 2$: $y_1 + y_3 = 4$ for $(1,3), (2,2), (3,1)$ — 6 good; $y_2 = 3$: only $(3,3)$ — 8 good. Total $22$.

**Answer: (D) 22**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-24.title: Incentre
kangaroo-at-2016-student-24.body:
The angle bisectors meet at the incentre $P$, which has the same distance $r = \sqrt8$ from all three sides. The feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ to the legs $AB$ and $AC$ together with $A$ and $P$ form a square of side $r$ (the angle at $A$ is $90^\circ$). $PA$ is its diagonal: $PA = r\sqrt2 = \sqrt{16} = 4$.

**Answer: (E) 4**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-24.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2016-student-24.body:
Place $A$ at the origin with the legs on the axes. The incentre is $(r, r)$ with $r = \sqrt8$, so $PA = \sqrt{r^2 + r^2} = \sqrt{16} = 4$.

**Answer: (E) 4**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-25.title: Vieta
kangaroo-at-2016-student-25.body:
For $x^2 + ax + b = 0$ with roots $x_1, x_2$: $x_1^2 + x_2^2 = (x_1 + x_2)^2 - 2x_1x_2 = a^2 - 2b$. Similarly the second gives $b^2 - 2a$. Setting them equal: $a^2 - b^2 = 2b - 2a$, i.e. $(a - b)(a + b) = -2(a - b)$. Since $a \ne b$, $a + b = -2$.

(Such $a, b$ exist, e.g. $a = 0$, $b = -2$: $x^2 - 2 = 0$ and $x^2 - 2x = 0$ both have real roots, sums of squares $4$ and $4$.)

**Answer: (B) $-2$**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-25.title: Example check
kangaroo-at-2016-student-25.body:
With $a = 0$, $b = -2$: roots $\pm\sqrt2$ (squares sum 4) and $0, 2$ (squares sum 4). Then $a + b = -2$. The algebra above shows every valid pair gives the same sum.

**Answer: (B) $-2$**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-26.title: Opposite pyramids
kangaroo-at-2016-student-26.body:
Let the cube have edge $s$. Two pyramids on opposite faces have heights $h_1 + h_2 = s$, so together their volume is $\frac13 s^2 (h_1 + h_2) = \frac{s^3}{3}$. All three pairs of opposite pyramids have the same total volume.

The total is $42 + v$, so each pair sums to $\frac{42 + v}{3}$. Try to pair up $2, 5, 10, 11, 14$: $2 + 14 = 16$ and $5 + 11 = 16$, leaving $10 + v = 16$, so $v = 6$.

**Answer: (C) 6**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-26.title: Check the options
kangaroo-at-2016-student-26.body:
For each option the total $42 + v$ must be divisible by 3 and the six numbers must split into three equal-sum pairs: $v = 6$ gives pairs $\{2,14\}, \{5,11\}, \{10,6\}$, all with sum 16, and cube volume $48$. $v = 9$ gives total 51, pair sum 17: $2 + ? = 17$ needs 15 — impossible. $v = 12$: total 54, pair sum 18: $2 + 16$ — impossible. $v = 1$ and $v = 4$ give totals not divisible by 3.

**Answer: (C) 6**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-27.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2016-student-27.body:
Put $D = (0, 0)$, $C = (50, 0)$, $B = (50, 5)$, $A = (0, 5)$, so $M = (25, 0)$ and $N = (25, 5)$.

**First fold** ($B \to M$): the crease is the perpendicular bisector of $BM$. From $B - M = (25, 5)$ and the midpoint $(37.5, 2.5)$, the crease is $5x + y = 190$; it meets the top edge at $F = (37, 5)$ and the bottom edge at $(38, 0)$. The folded-over flap (grey side up) covers the part of the strip to the right of the segment $FM$.

**Second fold** ($D \to N$): the crease is $5x + y = 65$, meeting the bottom edge at $G = (13, 0)$ and the top at $(12, 5)$. The flap covers the part of the strip to the left of the segment $GN$.

The visible white part is the parallelogram $G M F N$ with vertices $(13, 0), (25, 0), (37, 5), (25, 5)$: base $12$, height $5$, area $60$ cm².

**Answer: (B) 60 cm²**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-28.title: p must be n + 1
kangaroo-at-2016-student-28.body:
The sum is $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$. Since $p$ divides none of $1, \dots, n$, we have $p > n$, so $p \nmid n$ and $p$ must divide $n + 1$ (it divides $n(n+1)$). As $p > n$, this means $p = n + 1$. So $n + p = 2p - 1$ with $p$ prime (and $p$ odd, since $p = 2$, $n = 1$ gives sum 1).

Check $p = \frac{(n+p)+1}{2}$: $217 \to 109$ (prime ✓), $221 \to 111 = 3\cdot 37$, $229 \to 115 = 5 \cdot 23$, $245 \to 123 = 3 \cdot 41$, $269 \to 135 = 5 \cdot 27$.

**Answer: (A) 217**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-28.title: Verify the example
kangaroo-at-2016-student-28.body:
$n = 108$, $p = 109$: the sum $1 + \dots + 108 = \frac{108\cdot109}{2} = 54 \cdot 109$ is divisible by the prime 109, and 109 divides none of $1, \dots, 108$. Then $n + p = 217$.

**Answer: (A) 217**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-29.title: An 8-move solution
kangaroo-at-2016-student-29.body:
Number rows and columns 1–5; the target has the 12 fields with $r + c$ odd black. Use these 8 moves:
- the four border triples in the middle of each side: row 1 columns 2–4, row 5 columns 2–4, column 1 rows 2–4, column 5 rows 2–4;
- four triples meeting at the centre: row 3 columns 1–3, row 3 columns 3–5, column 3 rows 1–3, column 3 rows 3–5.

Count how often each field is flipped: the centre is flipped 4 times (white); the middles of the border sides $(1,3), (3,1), (3,5), (5,3)$ are flipped twice (white); every other field touched is flipped exactly once, and these are exactly the 12 fields $(1,2), (1,4), (2,1), (2,3), (2,5), (3,2), (3,4), (4,1), (4,3), (4,5), (5,2), (5,4)$ — the black fields of the target. Corners and the fields $(2,2), (2,4), (4,2), (4,4)$ are never touched (white). So 8 moves suffice, which is less than 10. (A computer search confirms that 7 moves are not enough, so the minimum is exactly 8.)

**Answer: (A) less than 10**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-30.title: Product of all divisors
kangaroo-at-2016-student-30.body:
The divisors of $N$ pair up as $d$ and $\frac Nd$, so the product of all six divisors is $N^3$. Hence $N^3 = 648 \cdot d$ where $d$ is the missing divisor. $648 = 2^3 \cdot 3^4$. A number with six divisors is $p^5$ or $p^2q$. Trying $N = 18 = 2\cdot 3^2$: $N^3 = 5832 = 648 \cdot 9$, so $d = 9$ — and 9 does divide 18. (For $N = 12$: $1728/648$ is not an integer.)

**Answer: (C) 9**

kangaroo-at-2016-student-30.title: Direct check
kangaroo-at-2016-student-30.body:
The divisors of 18 are $1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18$, and $1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 6 \cdot 18 = 648$. The missing one is 9. Since $648 = 2^3\cdot 3^4$ only involves the primes 2 and 3, $N$ must be $2^5$, $3^5$, $2^2\cdot 3$ or $3^2 \cdot 2$; only $18$ works.

**Answer: (C) 9**
